tldr: We propose a framework where an LLM invents unprecedented cooperative motions from scratch—such as using a partner's back as a stepping stone to climb high ledges—and combines code-based kinematic interpolation, local optimization, and trajectory optimization to automatically generate dynamically feasible whole-body trajectories.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of the proposed framework, CoTAMP. Purple LLM modules handle coarse planning and keyframe generation at crucial points, while orange code-based modules take care of validation, interpolation, local optimization, and whole-body dynamic trajectory optimization (TO).
overview:
A single quadruped robot cannot scale ledges higher than its leg reach or cross wide gaps. But with two robots, one can crouch to serve as a stepping stone or bridge, letting the other climb on its back to overcome extreme terrain. Solving such cooperative tasks involving physical contact requires cooperative TAMP (Task and Motion Planning), which simultaneously solves high-level task planning ("who supports whom and in what order") and continuous motion planning ("where to place feet on the partner's back").

Traditional TAMP and recent LLM-based robotics research typically select and combine actions from a limited, predefined skill set (e.g., walk, sit, stand). However, that cannot handle unprecedented motions like climbing onto a partner's back. In this work, the authors take an approach where the LLM is not restricted to a predefined skill set, but instead invents the required motions freely.

Specifically, the LLM splits the entire task into individual motions (solo) and cooperative motions (coupled), establishing boundary poses. In subsequent motion generation, the LLM does not output trajectories across all timesteps. Instead, it only outputs "keyframes" where all feet are in contact. Dense intermediate motions are then quickly synthesized by mathematical code using Hermite interpolation and B-spline local optimization. Finally, trajectory optimization (TO) accounting for contact forces and torque limits ensures dynamic consistency.

When evaluated on three challenging simulation courses with two quadruped robots, the framework produced kinematically valid references in all 30 trials, and trajectory optimization converged in 100% of them. Compared to a baseline that prompts an LLM to generate the full trajectory in a single call, it achieves dramatically higher success rates and dynamic feasibility, while significantly reducing computation time and API costs.
contributions: Built a task planner that does not rely on a fixed skill set; the LLM invents physical contact and cooperation motions from scratch and automatically breaks them down into parallelizable steps.

Proposed a motion generator that has the LLM output only keyframes with four-foot contact, while code synthesizes intermediate trajectories via kinematic interpolation and local optimization, cutting token consumption and generation time while synthesizing dense motion.
Unified timelines by explicitly separating solo and coupled motions, eliminating unnecessary idle waiting between robots and cutting task execution time by up to 43%.

Demonstrated on three challenging courses where two quadruped robots use each other as stepping stones and bridges that dynamically feasible whole-body trajectories converge under trajectory optimization (TO) in all 30 out of 30 trials.

sections.heading: Using a partner as a stepping stone: the cooperative TAMP challenge
sections.summary: Overcoming terrain impassable for a single robot requires advanced cooperative TAMP. Moving away from fixed skill catalogs, this new framework lets an LLM invent motions freely while mathematical optimization guarantees dynamic feasibility.
sections.details:
TAMP (Task and Motion Planning) has gained attention as a way for legged robots to navigate complex obstacles. However, many environments are physically impossible for a single robot, such as ledges exceeding leg length or wide crevasses. If two robots team up, one can act as a stepping stone (Fig. F1) or bridge, allowing the partner to climb onto its back and move ahead.

Classical TAMP and recent LLM-based planning methods mostly select actions from human-designed skill sets (e.g., "walk," "sit," "stand"). This setup cannot produce complex contact motions that were not anticipated in advance, such as "climbing onto a partner's back" or "the supported robot shifting its posture while holding load."

Therefore, the authors chose to let the LLM invent necessary motions on the fly rather than picking fixed skills. However, asking an LLM to write full-body trajectories over long horizons causes token explosions and physical breakdowns (e.g., floating in mid-air, violating joint limits). To resolve this, they adopted a hybrid setup: the LLM handles global planning and keyframes where all four feet touch the ground, while code handles dense intermediate trajectories using kinematic interpolation, local optimization, and trajectory optimization (TO). This achieves high success rates and physical feasibility while keeping computational costs low.

captions.F1: Motion trajectory generated by the framework in Course 1. The blue robot uses the red robot's back as a stepping stone to climb the high ledge, after which both reach their respective goals.

sections.heading: The frontier of LLMs in robotics and where this work stands
sections.summary: Existing research spans LLM-based task planning, controller design, and direct motion generation. This work stands apart by addressing coupled motions where multiple robots physically support each other's loads.
sections.details:
This section categorizes related research into three streams and clarifies how the proposed method differs.

### II-A LLM-Based Planning
Classical TAMP combines symbolic search with continuous geometric computation, but action definitions were rigid. While recent LLM-based planners enable flexible reasoning, most still call pre-trained RL skills or predefined APIs. In contrast, this work maintains no predefined skill catalog and invents physical contact motions between two robots from scratch through free-form text.

### II-B LLM-Designed Controllers
Many works prompt LLMs to write MPC (Model Predictive Control) cost functions or RL reward functions. However, these target single robots. Designing consistent contact sequences and full-body trajectories for two robots physically contacting and loading each other remained difficult.

### II-C Direct Motion Generation
Recent studies have explored having LLMs directly generate end-effector trajectories or joint angle time series as code. Yet these also assume a single manipulator or single legged robot. When one robot steps onto another's back, the supporting robot's legs compress and contact states become tightly coupled, making single-robot direct generation unusable. This work is the first attempt to generate mutually dependent, coupled motions between two robots without failure.

sections.heading: Challenging courses for two quadruped robots and the overall pipeline
sections.summary: Targeting two RAIBO2 robots with 12 joints each, three environments were created that cannot be cleared without cooperation. The pipeline is hierarchical, pairing LLM reasoning with code-based rigor.
sections.details:
### III-A Problem Setting
The evaluation uses two "RAIBO2" quadruped robots (blue and red), each with 3 degrees of freedom per leg for a total of 12 actuators. Besides static obstacles, environments contain movable boxes sliding on 1-DOF rails. The termination condition is met when both robots stand in their color-matched goal regions. All three courses (Fig. F2) are physically impossible for a single robot, making cooperation mandatory.

- Course 1: Contains a high ledge requiring one robot to climb using its partner's back as a stepping stone.
- Course 2: Contains a wide crevasse where a partner must bridge the gap so the other can cross over it.
- Course 3: A puzzle-like environment where a robot pushes a box to rescue a trapped partner, then moves boxes to build a bridge across a gap.

### III-B Pipeline
The overall system has the hierarchical structure shown in Fig. F3. First, "Task Planning" divides the entire task into multiple steps and determines boundary poses. Next, "Motion Generation" generates motions for each step in parallel. Finally, "Trajectory Integration" merges them onto a single timeline and applies trajectory optimization (TO) to produce dynamically feasible continuous trajectories. The key is cleverly dividing work between LLM reasoning and code-based geometric validation, interpolation, and optimization.

captions.F2: The three cooperative courses used in experiments. From left to right: (a) Course 1, climbing using the partner's back as a stepping stone; (b) Course 2, crossing a crevasse using the partner's back as a bridge; (c) Course 3, pushing boxes to rescue a partner and build a bridge.

sections.heading: Task planning: inventing motions and dividing them into steps
sections.summary: The LLM task planner takes environment information and defines an execution order and boundary poses combining solo and coupled motions. It iterates revisions until passing code-based geometric and structural checks.
sections.details:
### IV-A Inputs
The task planner receives obstacle data in JSON, robot models in URDF format, a rendered image of the initial state, an output schema, and prompts.

### IV-B Plan Representation
The plan output by the planner contains:
- Step sequences for each robot (whether it is a "solo step" involving only one robot or a "coupled step" where both contact and cooperate, along with the reason for cooperation)
- Motion category for each step (free-form text)
- Precedence constraints between steps (e.g., "Blue Step 2 cannot start until Red Step 1 finishes")
- Required object (box) state changes
- Robot poses at the start and end of each step (stable standing poses with nominal joint angles and a horizontal torso)

There is no predefined skill set. The LLM inspects the environmental geometry and invents the motion itself, deciding, for instance, "it needs to step on the back here."

### IV-C Plan Validation
The generated plan is rigorously verified by code-based modules. This involves two stages: (1) structural checks verifying step ID consistency, absence of cycles in the directed graph, and valid box movement order; (2) geometric checks ensuring all four feet are supported, collisions are avoided, and the final goals are reached at step boundaries. If validation fails, error details and rendered images of the failed state are sent back to the LLM for correction.

sections.heading: Motion generation: keyframe outputs and kinematic local optimization
sections.summary: Because start and end poses are fixed for each step, all steps can be generated rapidly in parallel. Standard walking is handled by rules, while challenging motions use LLM keyframes and B-spline local optimization to avoid collisions.
sections.details:
### V-A Inputs & V-B Motion Representations
Each step generator receives boundary poses, environment info, geometric constraints, and APIs for IK and collision checking. The authors use a smart binary choice depending on motion difficulty:
- Walking route: For simple translations or turns on flat ground, the LLM outputs torso waypoints, and a rule-based generator produces periodic walking at $0.8\,\mathrm{m/s}$ linear and $1.4\,\mathrm{rad/s}$ angular speed.
- Keyframes: For complex steps such as climbing ledges or inter-robot contact, the LLM outputs keyframes at critical points. Keyframes are restricted only to moments where all four feet touch surfaces, defining foot placement and torso pose. By avoiding writing every timestep, token usage is drastically reduced.

### V-C Kinematic Synthesis
Keyframes are smoothly interpolated using Hermite curves (torso) and semi-elliptical trajectories (swing feet). However, simple geometric interpolation can cause feet to catch on obstacle corners or exceed joint limits. To fix this, only the failing segment is locally optimized using B-spline curves to automatically clear obstacles (Fig. F4).

### V-D Validation, Correction, and Replanning
The synthesized trajectory is inspected every $10\,\mathrm{ms}$ for joint limits, contact support, collisions, and support margin. If it fails, the LLM is prompted up to two times with failure images to regenerate. If still unresolved (e.g., trying to climb a height impossible for one robot alone), it is flagged as a plan defect and sent back to the task planning stage for replanning (up to one time).

captions.F4: Mechanism of kinematic local optimization. While keeping surrounding keyframes fixed, only the segment where interpolation failed due to collisions (light orange region) is optimized by adjusting B-spline control points into a safe path.

sections.heading: Trajectory integration: eliminating idle waiting and satisfying dynamics
sections.summary: Independent step trajectories are placed onto a global timeline, removing unnecessary idle time. The resulting kinematic reference trajectory serves as an initial guess for trajectory optimization (TO) considering contact forces and torque limits.
sections.details:
Individually generated step trajectories are combined into a final single trajectory via a two-stage process.

### Composition
Each robot executes its assigned steps continuously without pauses. Waiting occurs only in two situations: when waiting for the partner's step due to a precedence constraint, or when arriving early before a coupled step. As shown in Fig. F5 (a), because solo steps proceed independently, total execution time is greatly reduced compared to an approach that makes robots wait after every step (Fig. F5 (b)).

### Trajectory Optimization
Even if a kinematically valid reference trajectory is constructed, it might violate motor torque or friction limits. Trajectory optimization (TO) is solved using Pinocchio for rigid body dynamics, CasADi for nonlinear optimization, and IPOPT as the interior-point solver. Because the kinematic reference trajectory provides an excellent initial guess, contact sequences are fixed, making nonlinear optimization converge reliably. To avoid having too many variables across long courses, trajectories are divided into time windows and solved sequentially.

captions.F5: Schematic of step scheduling on the global timeline. (a) In the proposed method, separating solo and coupled steps ensures waiting occurs only when synchronization is required. (b) If all steps are treated as coupled, a robot finishing early must wait for the other every time, introducing excessive idle time.

sections.heading: Experimental setup: rigorous sandboxed testing with Codex
sections.summary: Using gpt-6.1-sol in a secure sandbox without external code access, the authors evaluated five research questions across four metrics: success rate, dynamic convergence, time, and cost.
sections.details:
### VII-A LLM Settings
The LLM modules ran `gpt-6.1-sol` (reasoning effort: medium) via Codex CLI. To prevent the LLM from inspecting code outside its working directory, seeing other steps' results, or reading validation scripts, it was isolated in non-interactive bubblewrap sandboxes. Each trial was fully independent, with no prompt or response reuse across runs.

### VII-B Experiments & VII-C Metrics
The experiments evaluated five questions (Q1–Q5):
- Q1: Can the proposed method complete cooperative TAMP end-to-end?
- Q2: Does it outperform a single-call LLM baseline (Barebone)?
- Q3: Does solo/coupled decomposition reduce execution time?
- Q4: Is keyframe generation more time- and cost-efficient than full trajectory generation?
- Q5: Does kinematic local optimization improve synthesis success?

Metrics measured include: Kinematic success (passing geometric and kinematic checks), TO convergence (TO converging while satisfying constraints), Generation time (wall-clock time before TO), Cost (API usage cost), and Execution time (total duration of physical robot motion).

sections.heading: Results: 100% TO convergence and overwhelming generation efficiency
sections.summary: TO converged in all 30 trials, vastly outperforming single LLM calls. Separating solo motions reduced execution time by up to 43%, and keyframe generation cut API costs and generation time by around 40%.
sections.details:
### VIII-A Overall Performance (Q1)
Across 10 runs per course (30 total), the proposed framework generated geometrically valid reference trajectories in all 30 trials, and trajectory optimization (TO) converged 100% of the time. Average generation time ranged from 13.5 to 15.3 minutes, while generated motion execution times were 53 to 70 seconds.

### VIII-B Comparison with Single LLM Calls (Barebone) (Q2)
Compared to a Barebone baseline generating coordinates for both robots and boxes in a single prompt, Barebone occasionally passed kinematic checks (6/10, 7/10, 10/10 across Courses 1–3). However, in Courses 1 and 2 involving contact climbing, Barebone produced physically impossible jumps, resulting in catastrophic TO convergence rates of 0/6 and 2/7. This proves that kinematic validation alone is insufficient; dynamic verification via TO is essential for contact-rich cooperative tasks.

### VIII-C Impact of Solo/Coupled Decomposition (Q3)
Compared to an All-coupled baseline treating every step as synchronized (Fig. F6), the proposed method reduced execution time by about 25% in Course 1, 26% in Course 2, and 43% in Course 3 (70.1 s vs. 123.3 s). In Course 3, where box-pushing takes long, concurrency provided massive gains. Generation time also dropped by 19–42% because fewer degrees of freedom were evaluated per LLM call.

### VIII-D Keyframes vs. Full Trajectory Generation (Q4)
On six representative difficult steps (Fig. F7), keyframe generation was compared against prompting the LLM to write 10 ms full trajectories. Both eventually succeeded, but keyframes cut generation time by ~38% and API cost by ~41% (Fig. F8). For long-contact motions like climbing the partner's back (Coop. ascent), it cut generation time by ~50% and cost by ~57%.

### VIII-E Impact of Kinematic Local Optimization (Q5)
Comparing keyframe interpolation with and without B-spline local optimization, interpolation alone succeeded in only 30 of 60 trials, with 0% success on steps with height variations or contact (e.g., ledge climbing and cooperative ascent). Adding local optimization achieved 60/60 (100%) success, proving its critical role in realizing difficult motions.

captions.F6: Comparison of task execution times between the proposed method (Ours), which separates solo and coupled steps, and the All-coupled baseline, which synchronizes every step. Idle time was reduced across all courses, cutting execution time by about 43% in Course 3.
captions.F7: Six representative motions used in step-level evaluations. Top row: two coupled steps with inter-robot contact (climbing and bridging). Bottom row: four solo steps (high platform ascent, pillar crossing, box pushing, maze walking).

sections.heading: Discussion and limitations: ideal division of labor between LLMs and code
sections.summary: Letting LLMs handle global decisions and keyframes while code ensures dense consistency and dynamics proved powerful. However, limitations remain: a two-robot design, ~15-minute planning times, and lack of real-robot tests.
sections.details:
The experimental results highlight the importance of properly delegating tasks between LLMs and mathematical code. Discrete, high-level choices like task decomposition and keyframe selection leverage the LLM's reasoning strength. Conversely, dense geometric consistency, collision avoidance, joint limits, and contact force/torque constraints should be left to mathematical code: interpolation, B-spline optimization, and IPOPT-based TO. Blurring these boundaries causes physical failure (like Barebone) or exploding computation costs (like Full-trajectory).

However, several clear limitations are noted:
- Number of robots: The current design is specialized for two robots. Handling three or more robots interacting simultaneously requires expanding coupled step representations.
- Long planning time: Even with parallel step generation, generating a valid trajectory takes ~15 minutes on average. Most of this is LLM inference latency, making it unsuitable for real-time online replanning under sudden disturbances.
- Lack of real-robot validation: Experiments were limited to three simulated courses. Robustness to real-world contact slip, hardware limits, and modeling errors remains future work.

sections.heading: Conclusion and future outlook
sections.summary: We proposed CoTAMP, blending LLM-invented cooperative motions with code-based kinematic and dynamic corrections. Achieving 100% success across 30 trials on three tough courses, future work aims at multi-robot scaling and physical hardware tests.
sections.details:
This paper presented CoTAMP, a new cooperative task and motion planning framework for two quadruped robots. Without relying on fixed skill sets, an LLM flexibly invents high-level plans and keyframes, while code modules handle geometric validation, interpolation, local optimization, and trajectory optimization (TO).

Simulation experiments on challenging courses proved that it drastically outperforms single-call LLM baselines, cuts unnecessary waiting, and achieves substantial time and cost reductions via keyframes. Future work will extend the framework to three or more robots, reduce LLM latency, and validate the system on physical hardware in the real world.

takeaways: Do not make LLMs write dense, long-horizon trajectories directly: having LLMs output only high-level task decompositions and contact-switch keyframes—while delegating intermediate motions to interpolation and local numerical optimization—is the most robust and cost-effective approach.

Kinematic validity is completely different from dynamic feasibility: experiments show over half of trajectories passing kinematic checks fail when subjected to trajectory optimization (TO) considering contact forces and torque limits, proving TO validation is vital for cooperative legged robots.

Explicitly separate solo and coupled motions: synchronizing robots across every step creates massive idle waiting times; isolating parallelizable solo segments cuts real-world execution time by over 40%.
limitations: Plan generation takes about 15 minutes, mostly due to LLM API call latency, preventing rapid online replanning in response to real-time environmental changes.
The formulation is specialized for two-robot cooperation and cannot be directly applied to large-scale multi-robot cooperation involving three or more robots interacting simultaneously.
Evaluations remain confined to physics simulation; experiments under real quadruped hardware constraints and contact friction variations have not yet been conducted.
